content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an adversarial algorithm for training RL agents in multi-task settings called ATE-PPO. The authors show that this leads to learning multiple solutions for a given task and outperforming a non-adversarial baseline. They evaluate their approach on a number of continuous control environments including a subset of the tasks in Meta World.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths: 
- mostly clear, well-written paper
- promising initial results compared with a simple non-adversarial baseline
- some interesting connections to causality

# Weaknesses
- some claims are false e.g. first adversarial method for MTRL
- not enough baselines and ablations to judge the effectiveness of the work
- no evaluation on well-established benchmarks
- a lot of missing related work 
- not enough details about the experimental setup

Please see below for more details on each of the above.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# Clarity
1. The paper is clear and well-written overall. While I didn't find any major issues regarding clarity, there are a few minor places where the writing could be further improved, as explained below.

2. One thing I was confused about was the use of multi-task RL. However, in the first experiment on Point Mass it seems like it is a single task with multiple solutions. Can you please clarify this and make sure you use the term consistently throughout the paper?

3. The authors shouldn't assume all readers are familiar with TE-PPO since that makes it difficult to understand the contribution and what exactly the base algorithm is doing. I recommend adding enough details about TE-PPO so that the paper is self-contained and readers don't have to go read that paper in order to understand this work. 

# Quality 
1. The paper could benefit from a more thorough empirical evaluation. The current experiments are not enough to fully support the claims and warrant acceptance at the ICLR conference. To begin with, the only baseline used is TE-PPO, which is non-adversarial, doesn't do any fancy exploration, and is not the most effective existing method for this setting. I suggest the authors to include more baselines such as [1], [2], [4], [5], or [7]. 

2. The approach is only evaluated on a few toy-ish settings and a few tasks from Meta World selected by the authors. Why not evaluate it on the full Meta World settings MT10 or MT50? This would make the paper much stronger since the evaluation would be on an established benchmark and would allow comparison with many other approaches. Otherwise, how can one know whether the tasks weren't cherry picked to make your approach look better. 

3. The experimental setup also seems to be missing important details such as the number of seeds used. For example, Figure 2 doesn't seem to display standard deviation. How many seeds have you used?

4. Can you comment on the relationship between this approach and MaxEnt? it seems like something like MaxEnt or [9] could be helpful in this setting. I recommend including these as baselines and adding a discussion regarding this. 

5. In Figure 2b, TE-PPO and ATE-PPO look similar. However, you claim that TE-PPO cannot discover multiple solutions without the adversarial component. However, it seems to be able to do so and the two policies look quite similar -- I imagine the difference could be due to not enough training of TE-PPO or the training seed. 

6. The variance of ATE-PPO in Figure 5 seems quite high and much larger than that of TE-PPO. Do you understand why that is?

# Novelty
1. The proposed approach is novel as far as I can tell. However, the authors claim that this is "the first adversarial training regime for multi-task RL", which is not entirely true. Depending on how exactly we define adversarial training and multi-task RL, there have been multiple works applying something like this in RL, such as Dennis et al. 2020 [3], Parker-Holder et al. 2022 [6], OEL Team 2021 [7], or Jiang et al. 2021 [8] (to name just a few). Hence, the authors need to make the "novelty" claims more specific and tone them down in order to ensure their accuracy. 

2. The paper is missing many relevant works on e.g. adversarial training in RL such as [1], [2], [4], [5], in addition to the ones mentioned above. I recommend doing a more thorough literature review on adversarial training in RL. I also suggest discussing how ATE-PPO differs from prior work in greater detail. Many of the existing approaches are similar enough that they should be used as baselines e.g. [1], [2], [5], [7], [8]. Otherwise, it is difficult to assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach relative to prior methods.  

# Reproducibility
While the paper contains a reasonable amount of detail regarding the experiments and implementation, I believe it will be difficult to reproduce the results without access to the code. Can the authors comment on their plans of open sourcing the code? This is an important factor in deciding whether to accept the paper or not. 

### References
[1] Robust Adversarial Reinforcement Learning, Pinto et al. 2017

[2] Robust Reinforcement Learning using Adversarial Populations, Vinitsky et al. 2020

[3] Emergent Complexity and Zero-shot Transfer via Unsupervised Environment Design, Dennis et al. 2021

[4] Robust Deep Reinforcement Learning with Adversarial Attacks, Patannaik et al. 2017

[5] Evolving Curricula with Regret-Based Environment Design, Parker-Holder et al. 2022
 
[6] Open-Ended Learning Leads to Generally Capable Agents, OEL Team 2021

[7] Prioritized Level Replay, Jiang et al. 2020
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper contains some interesting ideas and aims to address an important problem, the experimental evaluation falls short of supporting the claims and being thorough enough to warrant acceptance at the ICLR conference. A large body of related work is not cited, discussed, or compared with, and some of the claims are false in their current form. I recommend taking into account the received feedback and submitting the paper to a future conference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to learn a robust policy by adding an adversarial attack on the skill space, not on the policy. More specifically, the proposed method perturbs the skill encoder to minimize rewards and mutual information between task $\tau$ and skill embedding $z$. The experiments show that the proposed method explores better to find multiple goals and transfers them better to unseen tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

* This paper proposes a novel approach to learning skill latents and a skill policy by adversarial training on the skill space.

* The paper is clearly written and easy to follow.

### Weaknesses

* The adversarial learning objective is to minimize the q-value and mutual information between $z$ and $\tau$. But, the second term in Eq (2) seems to maximize mutual information, which is conflicting with the explanation.

* The proposed causal effect estimation is useful to analyze the skill latents, but does not have a clear use case for the proposed problem.

* The experiments are too simple (a small number of task instances for each experiment) to verify their exploration capability and robustness.

* The exploration of the proposed method seems slightly better than the baseline TE-PPO. It might be also interesting to see whether the proposed adversarial training works better than simply adding noise to the skill space during training.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* As the paper has built on top of TE-PPO, it would be great to include an overview of TE-PPO (which is already in the method section) along with Figure 1(a) in the preliminaries.

* In the second line of Eq (4), where does $t$ come from? I think it should be $E_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} [\mathcal{I}(z;\tau) + \mathcal{I}(\tau;z)]$.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an interesting idea to encourage exploration in multi-task RL. However, the experiments are insufficient to support the claim of the paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed an adversarial training approach for Multi-Task RL. The idea is to train two competing agents, one picking the policy and an embedding to optimizing rewards, while the other agent learns another embedding to minimize an adversarial loss function. Experiments demonstrate the performance of the proposed method on PointMass and 2-D navigation tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The proposed adversarial training architecture for task embedding is interesting, and the numerical results seem promising.

Weaknesses:
- Little discussion is provided on why the adversarial loss function is defined with the three entropy terms. Is minimizing the mutual information between the task and embedding actually gives better performance or the entropy term just simply provides regularization?
- The proofs in Appendix C are likely incorrect. For example, (19) directly sets the minimum to be the bound which won't be achieved in most cases.
- Despite presenting the causal perspective, the provided properties have little connection to the proposed adversarial training method, and there are no analysis evaluating the benefits of the adversarially trained embedding.
- In numerical experiments, only one baseline policy is compared. Since learning a good embedding for multi-task problems is one of the main feature of the proposed method, comparing with some embedding learning methods like variational inference based baselines is important.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper introduces several concepts like two-player minimax games and average causal effect, but their descriptions are not clear and many of the properties are actually very generic to adversarial training and variational inference methods.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of using adversarial training for Multi-Task RL could be promising, but the paper has some incorrect claims and does not have enough justifications for the benefits of the proposed method.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes the algorithm ATE-PPO, an extension to the pre-existing algorithm presented by Hausman et al. (2018), which is denoted TE-PPO (task embedding proximal policy optimization) in the paper under review and to my knowledge first in Yu et al. (2020). ATE-PPO adds an adversary that perturbs the task embeddings of the model intended for use on target tasks in order to improve the robustness and exploration of this model. The paper investigates the causality of latent embeddings as skills on tasks of interest by computing a form of what is known as the average treatment effect, or average causal effect in this paper as well as in Chattopadhyay et al. (2019) and using this to measure the "average importances" of embedding components. The paper evaluates ATE-PPO against TE-PPO on two toy problems and a small subset of Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020) tasks and shows that ATE-PPO outperforms TE-PPO and that the learned latent features are somewhat semantically-meaningful.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         

References

Chattopadhyay, Aditya, Piyushi Manupriya, Anirban Sarkar, and Vineeth N. Balasubramanian. "Neural network attributions: A causal perspective." In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 981-990. PMLR, 2019.

Hausman, Karol, Jost Tobias Springenberg, Ziyu Wang, Nicolas Heess, and Martin Riedmiller. "Learning an embedding space for transferable robot skills." In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018.

Yu, Tianhe, Deirdre Quillen, Zhanpeng He, Ryan Julian, Karol Hausman, Chelsea Finn, and Sergey Levine. "Meta-world: A benchmark and evaluation for multi-task and meta reinforcement learning." In Conference on robot learning, pp. 1094-1100. PMLR, 2020.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper motivates the problem it aims to address well. It is generally clearly written and Figures and Tables are illustrative and easy to understand. The proposed algorithm outperforms the baseline it is being compared against (though the former is an extension of the latter, so this doesn't seem surprising).

Questions or Room for Improvement:

1. Should the lowercase "t"s encountered first in Eq. (2) and the LHS of Eq. (4) be Taus? If so, should the "t" in the second mutual information term in the latter be "z"?
2. The paper would benefit from using more than just one baseline, especially when this baseline isn't currently considered state-of-the-art and since many other approaches use "latent skills for learning policy [sic]." This is because it is difficult to say how well the adversarial training regime would improve RL algorithms generally when it has been evaluated against only one baseline.
3. The results would be stronger (i.e., convincing that they apply more generally) if the domains that the algorithms were evaluated on were more challenging. The two toy problems are simple, and a tiny subset of Meta-World was used. Furthermore, these are all synthetic, or simulated, problems. There are no evaluations on real-world problems, and even though Meta-World roughly simulates real-world scenarios, again, only a tiny subset of it was used.
4. Figure 4 doesn't seem to well support the claim that the figure caption makes in its last sentence.
5. Is there any exploration as to why the "policy network can learn only the minimum number of skills required to solve the task"? The loss function of the protagonist seems like it wouldn't affect this. Does the adversary induce this effect?
6. Why does TE-PPO "serve[s] as the perfect baseline to showcase the effect of an adversarial training regime" (Section 2.1)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and Figures and Tables are illustrative and easy to understand. 

The quality and novelty are limited. There is a dearth of baseline algorithms and the problem domains lack challenge and diversity. Perturbing agents to improve their robustness and exploration is a long-standing idea. The use of causal attribution in reinforcement learning, especially for feature importances, which have been considered for decades now in machine learning generally, is of incremental novelty.

The reproducibility is very good. Model hyperparameters for experiments for each problem domain are provided in the Appendix.

Unfortunately, much of the paper text and equations closely match those of previous works. Just in the main body of the paper, half of Section 3 closely matches text in Hausman et al. (2018) and almost all of Section 4 closely matches text in Chattopadhyay et al. (2019). Especially for the latter, it would've been better to simply reference Chattopadhyay et al. (2019), as the text in Chattopadhyay et al. (2019) is more thorough and informative.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper does a good job motivating the problem, explaning the proposed algorithm, describing the experiments that it evaluates the algorithm and baseline in, analyzing certain results it obtains--especially around the attribute causal effect--and providing details needed to reproduce its results.

However, the quality and novelty of the algorithm and of the experiments are too low and limited in scope for me to recommend acceptance. I hope the authors apply their work to more diverse settings, especially some that involve real-world problems.
